This meeting is being recorded.
We have Justin as well.
Okay.
Bruce, nice to meet you.
Hi, Justin.
Hello, Justin.
Hey, guys.
Hey.
Good to meet you.
Hi, Justin.
How's it going?
Good to meet you.
Good to meet you finally.
There's been a lot of back and forth, but so glad this call is happening.
Thank you everyone for joining.
So, Justin, this call is really to connect you with Communimed founder Robin and for you to tell us a little bit more about Portrait Capital and your interest in Communimed.
So if you would like to start and tell us about your business and your interest in Communimed, then Robin can tell you more about Communimed.
Sure, that sounds good.
Good to meet you guys.
I'm Justin Burris.
I'm one of the co founders at Portrait.
We're a private investment firm.

Started the firm about five years ago now along with my partner Tim Ludwig, based in New York, but previously was with a larger investment firm, invested in founder and family owned companies really all over the world.

When we started the firm, it was pretty specifically with a thesis on supporting founder and family owned companies typically instead of niche essential service industries and really trying to build platforms for the long term.
So trying to roll up our sleeves and support growth.

Five of the six are in the U.S. one of them's up in Canada and they're in sort of smaller niche markets where we're typically kind of an early mover and professionalizing and laying the groundwork for growth.
You know, four of us on the team here in New York.
Here in California actually.
Sorry, my numbers are old.

and
my colleague Bruce is online.

Hi all.
Nice to meet you.
Yeah, my name is Bruce.
I did just move to Los Angeles from New York, but I've been on the team with Justin for about three years and excited to learn a little bit more about the business.
Nice to meet you, Bruce.
Yeah.
Well, that's awesome.
In a nutshell, Robin, it'd be great to hear a little bit of the background of building the business and where you guys are today.
Sure.
I mean, where we started this business 35 years ago, but prior to that.
So it's it, it's a family owned business.
It's myself and my wife who founded the business and we're equal shareholders in it.
Our, our background is we have, we're university graduates with science degrees and then with that we moved into pharmaceutical industry, so in various capacities, sales and marketing, et cetera.
And then from there went on to the.
The supplier side in the publishing and communication segments.
And then we, we met along that path.
And then after we got married, we decided that, you know, we really wanted to do something on our own.
So we actually started the business as a point of care.
You know, exactly the core of what you see now in the business.
This is how it actually started.
You know, poster printed poster programs that are fitted into dedicated frames, you know, within pharmacies.
That's how we started it.
And, you know, that expanded into clinics.
And we had various partners along the way that helped us sort of achieve growth across the country.
And then we sort of got into a lot of other things, medical education, and we were sort of spreading ourselves in a.
A lot of different areas.
And around 2016, we decided that we really needed to consolidate our efforts around the point of care.
And this was around the time point of care marketing, let's say this is really around the time that the point of care marketing channel in the US Is really starting to get rolling.
So really since then, we've just.
We sort of divested ourselves of all these other engagements that people still seem to want us to do.
But all of our efforts are focused on growing this network and developing expertise in that niche and dominating that particular segment, which is where we stand today.
We're really sort of standalone in Canada as being the most important player in that market.
So this is where we're at and happy to chat about details.
Interesting.

I'm just curious, like, some of the differences between point of care marketing in Canada versus the U.S. like, any differences in terms of regulation or what works or doesn't work or anything to be mindful of?
Yeah, yeah, sure.
There's.
There is some.
I guess there's three areas where they're very different.
One is the size.
So in the US you can get to a critical mass much more easily with different players in the US Than you can in Canada.
In the US you're allowed to advertise prescription drugs.
So I don't know, I'm sure you've seen them, right?
They're everywhere.
So you're.
You're bombarded with these prescription drug ads which, which.
So this opens up a whole.
A lot of opportunities in the US that we don't have in Canada.
In Canada, we have to be much more nuanced in terms of how we market pharmaceuticals.
We have to use a more indirect approach.

So companies would, let's say, see value in creating awareness about a particular condition that there was no treatment for or they would want the patients to look play a role in being more activated about knowing about other options that they may not have heard about.

There's various ways that you can achieve this objective here, but even though you're not speaking about branded medications, having said that, branded advertising performance for prescription drugs is allowed as long as you limit it to the name of the drug and, and its price, which no one talks about.
So you can kind of.
In Canada we have Ozempic, you know, ask your doctor about it and variations of that.
And if you're going to, you can't say Ozempic for diabetes or something for some stuff like this.
That's the big difference.
There are ways to support it indirectly without talking about what it's for, which is something we do.
But you know, that's the way it's being done here.
And pharma is putting.
Is doing a lot of this right now, this branded but no context type advertising.
And we're actually trying to create a narrative with them that there's a benefit to having the unbranded coupled with branded elsewhere.
But that's just one the things we do.
So those are the differences.
Very different regulatory environment here compared to
the U.S. yeah, no, that, that makes sense.
That's very interesting.
And right now, just to understand.
So there's.
Well, I.
It might happen here.
The split between printed materials and screen is.
Screen is growing faster and it's becoming a larger portion of the business or how should I think about.

And I say digital, I mean the screens.
Right.
I'm talking about social media here.
Screens have had a surge in popularity because pharma has been very big on these branded ads.
So what tends to happen in pharma is, you know, let's say there's a new category of drug available.
There's usually two or three companies that happen to be coming along with these things in a similar time frame.
And they tend to get.
They feel that they've got to create awareness for the brand above all else and they don't want to develop the market if someone else stands to benefit.
So there is this issue which is popular right now.
You know, there's reason to believe that that may not be as popular in the future and that unbranded campaigns may start to take their role again.
But in this particular channel, I think it's important to Be able to be agile and to be able to do whatever the market is demanding of us.

Obviously, when you're in the point of care, when you're in the waiting room, you have an advantage over the same information that will be, that will be disclosed in social media or somewhere else where someone's passively sort of looking at their feed versus being in the office and actually being in the moment when you're thinking about your health and having this opportunity to actually talk about whatever you've been exposed to.
So that's where there's an advantage.
And we just feel, just, we know this is going to, it's growing in the US and we know it's going to get more traction here as we expand our influence.
Sure.
No, that makes sense.

Is that right?

Okay.

Let's say there's a network of clinics and this is one of the things they offer.
We are not allowed to pay doctors or pharmacists to make use of that space.
Fortunately, because it would be a lot less profitable, probably wouldn't be viable, but fortunately, for ethical reasons, we're not allowed to do it.
So pharma, certainly pharma would not be allowed to indirectly be seen putting money into a doctor's pocket through, you know, through what we're doing.
So strictly not allowed.
So it's value, value based alone.
They can, they can sign up for the program, they can get out of the program.

and they choose like.
Well, if you look at the overall number of clinics and pharmacies, for example, what percent of them do you think have point of care marketing today?
Well, in this, in the.

Sure.

Sure.

It's purely educational for their patients.
Exactly.
Okay.
Yep.

You mean a total spend of.
Total marketing spend?

We estimate the market size.

This, the way, this way they're able to hold the price point without reducing it.

Sure.

So it's one way to block the competition.

Sure.

I think last year they were close to 65%.
Got it.
Okay.

We know that because of the situation they were in with their product life cycle.
Got it.
Okay.
And then so they're, they're losing, they're losing patent.
So when that happens, you know, that's, that's what affects it.
Sorry to interrupt.
Got it.
Okay.
So then at that given point, there's probably one client that's a larger chunk.

Like, have there been instances in the past where like, there hasn't like been that natural moment for like one, one company to like step up and really be a large portion or it's always like you're going to expect, based on whatever the drug life cycle is that somebody's going to want to be more in market at that moment?
Well, it very much coincides with the, the opportunity that the company sees in the drug they have.

And you know, if you can get, if you can, if you can be part of their strategy.

summary.action_items:
**Justin Burris**
Follow up internally within Portrait Capital regarding strategic interest and next steps with Communimed (25:37)
summary.overview:
- **Investment Focus:** Portrait Capital values founder-owned niche businesses, currently managing six companies across the U.S. and Canada.  
- **Communimed’s Legacy:** Established 35 years ago, Communimed is focused on point-of-care marketing, dominating the Canadian market.  
- **Market Compliance:** Canada’s stricter pharma advertising rules shape Communimed's marketing, allowing for indirect educational campaigns.  
- **Growth Potential:** Communimed holds 15% market penetration in Canadian clinics, with a market size of about $40 million.  
- **Client Dependency:** One client contributes 65% of revenue; company plans to diversify as patents expire.  
- **Leadership Transition:** Founders aim for gradual transition, valuing legacy and seeking to maintain business importance.
summary.short_summary: The discussion highlighted Portrait Capital's strategic investment approach, emphasizing founder-owned niche businesses for long-term growth, with a portfolio of six companies in North America. Communimed's 35-year legacy as a family-owned healthcare marketing business was underscored, particularly its focus on point-of-care marketing, which dominates the Canadian market. Key differences between Canadian and U.S. pharmaceutical advertising regulations were addressed, illustrating the challenges Communimed navigates in its marketing strategies. The company's significant market penetration of 15% in Canadian clinics, reliance on a dominant client contributing 65% of revenue, and plans for diversification as patents expire were also discussed. The founders’ vision for a gradual transition of leadership that ensures the company's legacy underscores the collaborative nature of the meeting.
